new_d.text: The study of being; as a first approximation, Thomas Hofweber writes, “the study of what there is”, including “the study of the most general features of what there is”.

new_text.text: Aristotle opens Book IV of the Metaphysics with “a science which investigates being as being” (W. D. Ross's translation), and John Palmer, on his modal reading of Parmenides, sees Parmenides as “the founder of metaphysics or ontology as a domain of inquiry distinct from theology”.

The word, Peter van Inwagen, Meghan Sullivan and Sara Bernstein write, was invented at about the seventeenth century “to be a name for the science of being as such”, and Christian Wolff called the study of being as such general metaphysics, or ontology.

On Quine's criterion of ontological commitment (“On What There Is”, 1948), as Phillip Bricker sets it out, a theory is committed to the entities its bound variables must be capable of referring to if its affirmations are to be true; Filippo Casati and Naoya Fujikawa give the slogan it is popularized as: “To be is to be the value of a bound variable.”

W. J. Korab-Karpowicz calls the ontological difference, the distinction between being (das Sein) and beings (das Seiende), fundamental for Heidegger, and Mark Wrathall gives Heidegger's declared aim in Being and Time as “the concrete working out of the question of the ‘meaning’ (Sinn) of ‘being’”.

new_d.text: The branch of philosophy Aristotle called first philosophy, whose subject he identifies in one place as “being as such” and in another as “first causes”.

new_text.text: Peter van Inwagen, Meghan Sullivan and Sara Bernstein write that “Aristotle himself did not know the word”: an editor of his works, in all probability Andronicus of Rhodes, titled the fourteen books Ta meta ta phusika, after the books now called the Physics.

Michael Rohlf writes that Kant's Critique of Pure Reason seeks a “decision about the possibility or impossibility of a metaphysics in general” (Axii), and that its account makes transcendent metaphysics, a priori knowledge of things in themselves, impossible.

The logical positivists, van Inwagen, Sullivan and Bernstein write, concluded that metaphysical statements are meaningless, since they make no predictions about possible experience; Thomas Uebel reports Philipp Frank's suggestion (1963) that Carnap's “purely logical critique of metaphysics” of 1932 “was bound to remain ineffective as long as the actual use of metaphysics remained unexamined”.

Van Inwagen, Sullivan and Bernstein count theories of modality built on possible worlds, such as Kripke's, Plantinga's and Lewis's, as witnesses to “the resurgence of metaphysics in analytical philosophy” in the last third of the twentieth century.
W. J. Korab-Karpowicz summarizes Heidegger's later critique: metaphysics “reduces being to a being”, and “Insofar as being itself is obliterated in it, metaphysics is nihilism.”

Leonard Lawlor writes that Derrida speaks of “metaphysics” as if the Western philosophical tradition were uniform, and that he seems to have taken the word deconstruction from Heidegger's use of “destruction” in Being and Time.

new_d.text: A characteristic that belongs to a thing without being part of what the thing is said to be intrinsically: S. Marc Cohen and C. D. C. Reeve's example from Aristotle is that “pallor is an accidental characteristic of a man”.
In the modal sense Philip Atkins, Fabrice Correia and Teresa Robertson Ishii set out, an accidental property of an object is one that it “happens to have but that it could lack”.

new_text.text: In the Categories, as Paul Studtmann sets it out, Aristotle divides beings into ten categories: substance, quantity, quality, relatives, somewhere, sometime, being in a position, having, acting and being acted upon (1b25–2a4).

What is present in a subject, in something without being a part of it and unable to exist separately from it (1a24–5), is accidental, as Socrates' whiteness is; were primary substances not to exist, Aristotle says, no other entity would exist (2b6).
Studtmann calls this reading, on which what is said of a subject is universal and what is present in one is accidental, “by far the orthodox interpretation amongst Aristotle’s Medieval interpreters”.

Atkins, Correia and Robertson Ishii separate the modal sense from a whatness sense, on which an essential property is one that answers the question of what the object is, and give an example Kit Fine discusses in “Essence and Modality” (1994): being a member of the set whose sole member is Socrates is modally essential to Socrates without being whatness essential.

new_d.text: Properties, qualities or attributes that many particular things can share, such as redness or justice.

Realists, in the words of Francesco Orilia and Michele Paolini Paoletti, hold that universals “exist as mind-independent entities”; nominalism about universals, as Sam Cowling and Daniel Giberman state it, is “the thesis that there are no universals”.

new_text.text: Orilia and Paolini Paoletti call Plato's view, on which universals (Plato's ideas or forms) exist even if uninstantiated, transcendent realism, and the view Aristotle defended “in opposition to his master”, on which they exist only if instantiated by objects, immanent realism.

In Jowett's translation of the Republic, Socrates begins an inquiry “in our usual manner: Whenever a number of individuals have a common name, we assume them to have also a corresponding idea or form” (Book X).

Porphyry's Isagoge left open whether genera and species are real or “situated in bare thoughts alone”, among other questions that, Gyula Klima writes, proved “irresistible for his medieval Latin commentators, beginning with Boethius”.

In the usual classification of their answers, which Klima calls “rather crude”, realists assert “the existence of real universals in and/or before particular things”, conceptualists allow them only, or primarily, as concepts of the mind, and nominalists acknowledge only, or primarily, universal words.

For William of Ockham, Paul Vincent Spade, Claude Panaccio and Jenny Pelletier write, everything that exists in the created universe is a singular substance or a singular quality, and “the only real universals are universal concepts in the mind”, natural signs of several things at once.

Among contemporary views Cowling and Giberman describe trope theory, on which a trope is “a particular (i.e., non-universal) qualitative nature”, and resemblance nominalism, on which “qualitative classification is governed by primitive resemblance facts”.

new_d.text: Reasoning in which the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises: if the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false.

new_text.text: Igor Douven groups induction and abduction (inference to the best explanation) as non-necessary inferences and deduction as necessary inference, in which “the truth of the premises guarantees the truth of the conclusion”; induction and abduction are ampliative, their conclusions adding to what the premises logically contain.

Jc Beall, Greg Restall and Gil Sagi characterize logical consequence as “necessary truth preservation in virtue of form”, and note that all presentations of its rules rely on schemes, Aristotle's syllogistic being “a proud example”.

Spinoza's Ethics is built deductively: in Steven Nadler's account the first proposition follows from the definitions and axioms of Part One, and “every subsequent proposition can be demonstrated using only what precedes it”.

A proof system is sound with respect to a model-theoretic semantics, in Beall, Restall and Sagi's definitions, if every argument that has a proof in it is model-theoretically valid, and complete if every model-theoretically valid argument has a proof in it.
Juliette Kennedy writes that the main theorem of Gödel's dissertation (1929) was the completeness theorem for first-order logic, “Every valid logical expression is provable”.

His incompleteness theorems (1931) concern another sense of the word, which Panu Raatikainen states: a formal system is complete if for every statement of its language either the statement or its negation can be derived.

The first theorem shows that any consistent formal system within which “a certain amount of elementary arithmetic can be carried out” is incomplete in this sense, and the second that such a system cannot prove its own consistency.

new_d.text: In metaphysics, as Philip Atkins, Fabrice Correia and Teresa Robertson Ishii characterize it, “the doctrine that (at least some) objects have (at least some) essential properties”.
In the humanities, Cressida Heyes writes, the term is used more loosely, most commonly for “an illegitimate generalization about identity”.

new_text.text: Atkins, Correia and Robertson Ishii note that Saul Kripke (1972/1980) and Hilary Putnam (1975) made essentialist claims about, for example, cats and water, such as that in any possible world “anything that is not composed of molecules of H2O is not water”.

Heyes calls the word “another philosophical term of abuse, intended to capture a multitude of sins”, and reports the suggestion of “strategic essentialism”, which she credits to Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1990): treating an identity as uniform only for interim political goals, with no claim to any deeper authenticity.

Mari Mikkola reports feminist critiques of gender realism, the view that there is something women as women share, among them Judith Butler's that identity categories are always normative and so exclusionary.

Among the gender nominalists, who deny this, she places Iris Young, for whom women make up “a particular kind of social collective”, a series unified by practico-inert realities, and Natalie Stoljar, for whom anyone who resembles a woman paradigm closely enough belongs to the resemblance class woman.

Among the neo-gender realists she places Sally Haslanger, for whom gender is “a matter of occupying either a subordinate or a privileged social position”, women being those systematically subordinated along some dimension and marked for it by observed or imagined bodily features.

new_d.text: An intellectual movement that, in Kevin Aho's words, “exploded on the scene in mid-twentieth-century France”, when a generation was forced to confront “the anxiety-provoking givens of death, freedom, and meaninglessness”.
Its formula, “existence precedes essence”, is in Aho's words “arguably the unifying principle of existentialism”.

new_text.text: Aho traces the formula to Being and Time, where Heidegger writes “The ‘essence’ of Dasein lies in its existence”; Sartre goes on to say that there is no human nature, and that we are condemned to be free because “there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us”.

Kierkegaard and Nietzsche, in Steven Crowell's words, “came to be seen as precursors of the movement”: in Aho's account Kierkegaard aimed his scorn at Hegel's system and made Abraham a knight of faith “leaping” into a paradox (Fear and Trembling, 1843), and Nietzsche set against slave morality a master morality of those with “the self-directed power to create their own meanings and values” after the death of God.

In The Second Sex, Debra Bergoffen and Megan Burke write, Beauvoir uses the category of the Inessential Other to designate the situation of women; Camus's absurd, in Ronald Aronson's account, is the situation between our impulse to ask ultimate questions and the impossibility of any adequate answer.

The word was “first introduced by Marcel in 1943”, Aho writes, and only Sartre and Beauvoir among the movement's major contributors explicitly called themselves existentialists; Camus “denied being an existentialist” (Aronson), and in 1946 Heidegger rejected the label for his earlier work (Crowell).
